title: Machine Learning Design Patterns
subtitle: Solve the recurring problems of ML systems with proven patterns for representing data, framing problems, training, serving and reproducibility, and know what each one costs.
outcomes: Apply established design patterns to recurring ML problems, choosing each from a symptom and stating its trade-offs
Represent high-cardinality, interacting and multimodal data with hashed features, embeddings, feature crosses and multimodal inputs
Frame problems with reframing, multilabel outputs, ensembles and cascades
Make training robust and efficient with checkpoints, transfer learning and distribution strategies
Design resilient serving with stateless functions, keyed predictions and batch serving
Make pipelines reproducible with repeatable splits, workflow pipelines and point-in-time feature joins
prerequisites: Foundations of AI System Design, or equivalent experience framing, building and evaluating models with pandas and scikit-learn. Install Python 3.10 or newer, then: pip install pandas numpy scipy scikit-learn duckdb pyarrow joblib fastapi uvicorn httpx pytest. Every dataset is generated by the labs or ships with scikit-learn.
description:
Machine learning systems keep running into the same problems: a category with too many values to one-hot encode, a rare group of cases drowned out by the common ones, a week of training lost to a crashed machine, features computed one way in training and another in production, results nobody can reproduce. Design patterns are the field's accumulated answers, each a named problem with a proven solution and known trade-offs. This course teaches the core patterns from the catalogue made popular by Machine Learning Design Patterns (O'Reilly, 2020), in five groups: repeatable splitting and how to choose patterns; hashed features, embeddings, feature crosses and multimodal input; reframing, multilabel, ensembles and cascades; useful overfitting, checkpoints, transfer learning and distribution strategies; and stateless serving, batch serving, workflow pipelines and feature stores.

Every pattern is built and measured, not just described. You'll compare hashing with one-hot encoding as collisions rise, learn product embeddings from shopping baskets, build a cascade for catering orders and test it against a single flexible model, make an interrupted training run resume to the same weights, measure what a naive feature join leaks compared with a point-in-time ASOF join in DuckDB, and serve the model through a stateless, validated FastAPI function with keyed predictions, a batch job and a cached workflow pipeline. The capstone hands you a working but badly designed churn pipeline to refactor with the patterns it needs.

modules.title: Introduction to ML Patterns
modules.summary: What a design pattern is, why machine learning systems need their own, how the catalogue is organised, and how to choose a pattern from a symptom, practised on your first pattern: repeatable splitting.

lessons.title: What a design pattern is
objectives: Define a design pattern and its parts
Describe where design patterns come from and how ML patterns are catalogued
key_points: A design pattern names a problem that keeps recurring, describes a proven solution, and states the solution's trade-offs, so a team can reuse the thinking instead of rediscovering it.

The idea comes from architecture: Christopher Alexander's A Pattern Language (1977) described patterns for buildings and towns; Design Patterns (1994) by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides brought it to object-oriented software.

Machine Learning Design Patterns (Lakshmanan, Robinson and Munn, O'Reilly, 2020) catalogues 30 patterns in six groups: data representation, problem representation, model training, resilient serving, reproducibility and responsible AI.
This course describes every pattern the same way: its name, the problem, how the solution works, its trade-offs and alternatives, and related patterns. Your pattern cards follow that shape.
A shared vocabulary speeds up design reviews: "hash the referrer" or "this needs a point-in-time join" carries the problem, the solution and the risks in a few words.

lessons.title: Why ML systems need patterns
objectives: Explain how ML systems fail differently from ordinary software
Relate recurring ML problems to the patterns that address them
key_points: An ML system's behaviour comes from data as much as from code, so data changes, leakage and differences between training and serving can break a model without a line of code changing.

The paper Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (Sculley and colleagues, NIPS 2015) observed that model code is a small part of a real ML system, surrounded by data collection, feature extraction, serving and monitoring code.
The same paper named the CACE principle, Changing Anything Changes Everything: inputs interact, so altering one feature, threshold or data source can change the behaviour of the whole model.

Recurring problems include results that can't be repeated, vocabularies that break on new values, rare cases drowned out by common ones, lost training runs, and features computed differently in training and serving.
Every pattern adds code or infrastructure, so it has a cost; it earns its place when the problem it prevents is likely and expensive in the system in front of you.

lessons.title: Choosing and applying patterns
objectives: Choose a pattern from a symptom rather than from fashion
Apply the Repeatable Splitting pattern
Record pattern decisions with their trade-offs
key_points: Start from the symptom: name what is going wrong or what is at risk, then find the pattern that addresses it. Patterns that solve problems you don't have only add complexity.

Symptoms map to patterns: categories unseen at serving time suggest a hashed feature, a rare subgroup that behaves differently a cascade, lost training progress checkpoints, and features that differ between training and serving a feature store.
Patterns combine: a workflow pipeline can use repeatable splitting, a shared transformation and a feature store, and its model can be served by a stateless serving function and by batch serving.

Repeatable Splitting hashes a key such as a customer ID to decide each row's split, so the split is the same in every run and on every machine, rows of one customer stay together, and new rows don't move old ones.
Write each pattern decision into the design document with the alternative considered and the trade-off accepted, so later readers know why the system looks the way it does.

"""Lab 1: the problem behind the Repeatable Splitting pattern, and the pattern itself."""

import hashlib

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split


def make_rides(seed=11, n=2000):
    """Synthetic taxi rides: 300 regular customers, several rides each."""
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    return pd.DataFrame({
        "ride_id": np.arange(1, n + 1),
        "customer_id": [f"C{c:04d}" for c in rng.randint(1, 301, n)],
        "day": pd.Timestamp("2025-01-01") + pd.to_timedelta(rng.randint(0, 90, n), unit="D"),
        "fare": np.round(rng.gamma(3, 6, n), 2),
    })


def hash_bucket(key, buckets=100):
    """A stable bucket for a key: the same on every machine, in every run, in any language that has MD5."""
    # TODO: hash the key's UTF-8 bytes with hashlib.md5, turn the hex digest into an integer
    #       (int(digest, 16)) and return it modulo buckets. Don't use Python's built-in hash().
    return 0


def hash_split(df, key, test_percent=20):
    # TODO: True for rows whose key's bucket is below test_percent (those rows form the test set)
    return df[key].map(lambda k: False)


def main():
    rides = make_rides()

    # The problem: a random split changes from run to run and scatters each customer across both sides.
    test_a = set(train_test_split(rides, test_size=0.2, random_state=1)[1]["ride_id"])
    test_b = set(train_test_split(rides, test_size=0.2, random_state=2)[1]["ride_id"])
    print(f"Random split, two runs: the test sets share {len(test_a & test_b) / len(test_a):.1%} of their rides")
    random_test = rides["ride_id"].isin(test_a)
    both = set(rides[random_test]["customer_id"]) & set(rides[~random_test]["customer_id"])
    print(f"Random split: {len(both)} of {rides['customer_id'].nunique()} customers are in both train and test")

    # The pattern: hash a key that groups related rows, then cut the hash range.
    test = hash_split(rides, "customer_id")
    both = set(rides[test]["customer_id"]) & set(rides[~test]["customer_id"])
    print(f"Hash split on customer_id: test share {test.mean():.1%}, customers in both: {len(both)}")

    shuffled = rides.sample(frac=1, random_state=99)
    same = hash_split(shuffled, "customer_id").sort_index().equals(test)
    print(f"Same assignment after shuffling the rows: {same}")

    more = pd.concat([rides, make_rides(seed=12, n=500).assign(ride_id=lambda d: d["ride_id"] + 2000)])
    kept = hash_split(more, "customer_id").iloc[: len(rides)].equals(test)
    print(f"Existing rows keep their side when new rows arrive: {kept}")

    print(f"Bucket of C0042: {hash_bucket('C0042')}  (anyone, anywhere, gets the same number)")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

modules.title: Data Representation Patterns
modules.summary: Represent inputs so models can use them: hash high-cardinality categories, learn embeddings, cross features to capture interactions, and combine text, categories and numbers in one model.

lessons.title: Hashed feature
objectives: Explain the problems a hashed feature solves and the collisions it costs
Choose a stable hash and a number of buckets
key_points: The problem: a category with very many values, such as merchants or referrer sites, whose full vocabulary isn't known at training time and keeps growing, makes one-hot models large and breaks them when a new value arrives.

The solution: map each value to one of N buckets with a deterministic hash modulo N. The model learns a weight per bucket, and a value never seen in training still lands in a bucket instead of causing an error.

Use a stable hash: Python's built-in hash() of a string is salted differently in every process. MD5 or MurmurHash3, which scikit-learn's FeatureHasher uses, give the same bucket on every machine and in every run.
Collisions are the cost: values sharing a bucket share its weight. With many more buckets than values collisions are rare and accuracy approaches one-hot; with few buckets they blur the signal.
A new value inherits whatever its bucket learnt, which is noise for that value. Retrain regularly so new values earn weights of their own, and keep other inputs that carry signal for them.

lessons.title: Embeddings
objectives: Explain what an embedding is and three ways to learn one
Use embeddings to generalise from a few labelled items
key_points: An embedding maps a high-cardinality or unstructured input, such as a product ID, a word or an image, to a short dense vector, learnt so that items that behave alike end up close together.

Embeddings can be learnt inside a model (an embedding layer is a trainable lookup table), taken from a pretrained model, or learnt from co-occurrence, for example by factorising a product-by-basket matrix with truncated SVD.

They let knowledge spread: a classifier trained on the embeddings of a few labelled items generalises to unlabelled items with similar vectors, which one-hot IDs can't do, because every ID is equally far from every other.
The number of dimensions is a hyperparameter: too few lose information, too many cost memory and overfit. Compare a few sizes on validation data, and check that nearest neighbours make sense.
Version embeddings with the model that produced them: vectors from a retrained model live in a different space, so stored vectors, for example in a search index, must be recomputed together.

lessons.title: Feature cross
objectives: Build a feature cross and explain the interactions it captures
Control the cardinality a cross creates
key_points: A feature cross joins two or more categorical features into one, such as day type by time of day, so a model can learn a separate weight for each combination.
It lets simple models capture interactions: bikes are busy on weekday mornings but weekend middays, a pattern no sum of a day weight and a time weight can express.
Bucketise numbers first, then cross: latitude bins crossed with longitude bins form a grid of map cells, each with its own weight.
A cross has as many values as the product of its inputs' levels, so it is sparse and high-cardinality; combine it with hashing or embeddings, and with L1 or L2 regularisation.
Cross features whose interaction makes sense in the domain. Tree ensembles and neural networks learn some interactions on their own, but an explicit cross still helps when data is limited.

lessons.title: Multimodal input
objectives: Combine text, categories and numbers in one model
Test whether each kind of input earns its place
key_points: Many problems mix kinds of input, such as free text, categories, numbers, timestamps and images; the multimodal input pattern turns each into numbers and joins them for one model.
Each modality gets its own representation: TF-IDF vectors or embeddings for text, one-hot vectors or embeddings for categories, scaled numbers, and pretrained embeddings for images.
In scikit-learn, a ColumnTransformer applies a different transformer to each column, including a TfidfVectorizer on a text column, and stacks the results side by side for one estimator.
One input can also be represented two ways at once, such as a rating as a number and as a category, or text as TF-IDF vectors plus simple counts such as its length.

Check that each modality earns its place with an ablation: train with and without it on the same split. Every extra input is another pipeline to maintain and another way for training and serving to diverge.

"""Lab 2: four data representation patterns, each on a small synthetic problem built for it."""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from scipy import sparse
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.decomposition import TruncatedSVD
from sklearn.feature_extraction import FeatureHasher
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler, normalize


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- A. Hashed feature
def merchants_data():
    rng = np.random.RandomState(3)
    risk = rng.normal(-2.2, 1.2, 3600)               # each merchant's log-odds of a chargeback

    def make(n, known):
        m = rng.randint(0, known, n)
        amount = np.round(rng.gamma(2, 30, n), 2)
        y = (rng.rand(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(risk[m] + 0.01 * (amount - 60))))).astype(int)
        return pd.DataFrame({"merchant_id": [f"M{x:05d}" for x in m], "chargeback": y})

    return make(40000, 3000), make(8000, 3600)     # the test month brings 600 brand-new merchants


def part_a():
    train, test = merchants_data()
    new = ~test["merchant_id"].isin(set(train["merchant_id"]))
    print(f"A. {train['merchant_id'].nunique()} merchants in training; {new.mean():.0%} of test rows are new merchants")

    def auc(Xtr, Xte):
        model = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xtr, train["chargeback"])
        return roc_auc_score(test["chargeback"], model.predict_proba(Xte)[:, 1])

    ohe = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore").fit(train[["merchant_id"]])
    print(f"   one-hot      {len(ohe.categories_[0]):6d} columns (a vocabulary to store)  AUC "
          f"{auc(ohe.transform(train[['merchant_id']]), ohe.transform(test[['merchant_id']])):.3f}")
    ids = train["merchant_id"].drop_duplicates()
    for n in [256, 4096, 65536]:
        # TODO: hasher = FeatureHasher(n_features=n, input_type="string"); hash train and test merchant ids
        #       (each row is a list with one string: [[m] for m in ...]) into Xtr and Xte;
        #       then count the merchants that share a bucket: the column each id lands in is
        #       hasher.transform([[m] for m in ids]).indices
        Xtr = Xte = None
        shared = 0
        continue
        print(f"   hashed {n:6d} buckets, {shared:4d} merchants share a bucket          AUC {auc(Xtr, Xte):.3f}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- B. Embeddings
CATEGORIES = ["dairy", "bakery", "produce", "frozen", "drinks", "snacks", "household", "pet"]


def baskets_data():
    rng = np.random.RandomState(5)
    category = np.repeat(np.arange(8), 50)              # 400 products, 50 per hidden category
    rows, cols = [], []
    for b in range(1000):
        c = rng.randint(8)
        same = rng.choice(np.where(category == c)[0], rng.randint(2, 5), replace=False)
        other = rng.randint(0, 400, rng.randint(1, 5))
        for p in set(same) | set(other):
            rows.append(p)
            cols.append(b)
    product_by_basket = sparse.csr_matrix((np.ones(len(rows)), (rows, cols)), shape=(400, 1000))
    return product_by_basket, category


def part_b():
    product_by_basket, category = baskets_data()
    # TODO: learn 8-number embeddings: TruncatedSVD(n_components=8, random_state=0).fit_transform(product_by_basket),
    #       then normalize() the rows so a dot product is a cosine similarity
    emb = normalize(np.random.RandomState(0).rand(400, 8))     # placeholder: random vectors
    sims = emb @ emb.T
    np.fill_diagonal(sims, -1)
    top5 = np.argsort(-sims, axis=1)[:, :5]
    precision = (category[top5] == category[:, None]).mean()
    print(f"B. Embeddings: 400 products -> 8 numbers each; nearest 5 neighbours share the hidden category "
          f"{precision:.1%} of the time")

    perishable = np.isin(category, [0, 1, 2]).astype(int)    # dairy, bakery, produce
    rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
    labelled = rng.choice(400, 60, replace=False)            # only 60 products have been labelled by hand
    unlabelled = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(400), labelled)
    clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(emb[labelled], perishable[labelled])
    acc_emb = (clf.predict(emb[unlabelled]) == perishable[unlabelled]).mean()
    ids = np.arange(400).reshape(-1, 1)
    ohe = OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore").fit(ids[labelled])
    clf_id = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(ohe.transform(ids[labelled]), perishable[labelled])
    acc_id = (clf_id.predict(ohe.transform(ids[unlabelled])) == perishable[unlabelled]).mean()
    print(f"   'perishable?' for 340 unlabelled products: one-hot product id {acc_id:.1%}, embedding {acc_emb:.1%}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- C. Feature cross
def rentals_data(seed):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    n = 4000
    day = rng.choice(["weekday", "weekend"], n, p=[5 / 7, 2 / 7])
    period = rng.choice(["early", "midday", "evening", "night"], n)
    busy_p = {("weekday", "early"): 0.85, ("weekday", "evening"): 0.8, ("weekday", "midday"): 0.25,
              ("weekday", "night"): 0.05, ("weekend", "early"): 0.1, ("weekend", "midday"): 0.85,
              ("weekend", "evening"): 0.35, ("weekend", "night"): 0.15}
    p = np.array([busy_p[(d, t)] for d, t in zip(day, period)])
    return pd.DataFrame({"day_type": day, "period": period, "busy": (rng.rand(n) < p).astype(int)})


def part_c():
    train, test = rentals_data(1), rentals_data(2)
    for df in (train, test):
        df["day_x_period"] = df["day_type"]          # TODO: the feature cross: day_type + "_" + period
    for name, cols in [("separate one-hots", ["day_type", "period"]), ("with the cross", ["day_x_period"])]:
        model = make_pipeline(OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
        model.fit(train[cols], train["busy"])
        auc = roc_auc_score(test["busy"], model.predict_proba(test[cols])[:, 1])
        print(f"C. Busy hour, logistic regression, {name:<17} AUC {auc:.3f}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- D. Multimodal input
def messages_data(seed):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    n = 3000
    calm = ["how do I change my delivery address", "where can I find my invoice", "the app logged me out",
            "can I add a second card", "what time does support open", "please update my email address"]
    urgent = ["I was charged twice and want a refund", "my account was locked and I cannot pay",
              "the courier left my parcel open and items are missing", "I will contact my lawyer about this",
              "you cancelled my order without telling me", "the device arrived broken"]
    is_urgent = rng.rand(n) < 0.3
    text = np.where(is_urgent, rng.choice(urgent, n), rng.choice(calm, n))
    plan = rng.choice(["free", "plus", "business"], n, p=[0.6, 0.3, 0.1])
    tenure = np.round(rng.gamma(2, 8, n)).astype(int)
    logit = -2.3 + 2.4 * is_urgent + 1.6 * (plan == "business") - 0.04 * tenure + rng.normal(0, 0.5, n)
    escalate = (rng.rand(n) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-logit))).astype(int)
    return pd.DataFrame({"message": text, "plan": plan, "tenure_months": tenure, "escalated": escalate})


def part_d():
    train, test = messages_data(7), messages_data(8)
    branches = {
        # TODO: one ColumnTransformer branch per input: (name, transformer, columns)
        #   "text":   TfidfVectorizer() on the "message" column (a single column name, not a list)
        #   "plan":   OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore") on ["plan"]
        #   "tenure": StandardScaler() on ["tenure_months"]
        "plan": ("plan", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["plan"]),
    }
    return
    for name, parts in [("text only", ["text"]), ("tabular only", ["plan", "tenure"]),
                        ("text + tabular", ["text", "plan", "tenure"])]:
        prep = ColumnTransformer([branches[p] for p in parts])
        model = make_pipeline(prep, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(train, train["escalated"])
        auc = roc_auc_score(test["escalated"], model.predict_proba(test)[:, 1])
        print(f"D. Escalation, {name:<15} AUC {auc:.3f}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    part_a()
    part_b()
    part_c()
    part_d()

hints: FeatureHasher(input_type="string") expects each row as a list of strings: [[m] for m in ids].
A one-hot model has never seen the unlabelled products' IDs, so every one of them gets the same prediction.
In a ColumnTransformer, pass a text column's name as a string ("message"), not a list, because TfidfVectorizer expects one-dimensional input.

modules.title: Problem Representation Patterns
modules.summary: Frame the learning problem to fit the decision: reframe outputs, predict several labels at once, combine models in ensembles, and split a problem into a cascade of models.

lessons.title: Reframing
objectives: Reframe a regression as a classification over buckets, and the reverse
Use bucket probabilities to answer a business question directly
key_points: Reframing changes the form of a problem's output to fit how it is used: a regression can become a classification over buckets, and a classification can become a score that is thresholded later.

Buckets give a probability distribution: when outcomes cluster in two places, such as a bridge being open or closed, a regression predicts the average, a value that rarely happens, while buckets show both outcomes and their chances.
Bucket probabilities answer business questions directly: summing the buckets above 45 minutes gives the chance of a late delivery, which a single estimate can't.
Other ways to express uncertainty include quantile regression, for example GradientBoostingRegressor with loss="quantile", and predicting the parameters of a distribution.
Buckets lose precision within each bucket and their edges are a design choice; judge the reframed model on the metric the decision actually uses.

lessons.title: Multilabel
objectives: Distinguish multilabel from multiclass problems
Build and evaluate a multilabel classifier
key_points: In a multilabel problem an example can carry several labels at once, such as a ticket about billing and login; in a multiclass problem exactly one class is correct.
Represent the targets as a 0-or-1 matrix with a column per label; scikit-learn's MultiLabelBinarizer builds it from lists of labels.
Predict one yes-or-no output per label: a sigmoid output per label in a neural network, or a binary classifier per label with MultiOutputClassifier, with a threshold chosen for each label.
Evaluate with Hamming loss (the share of individual label decisions that are wrong), subset accuracy (every label exactly right, a strict measure) and micro- or macro-averaged F1.
Labels often depend on each other; ClassifierChain feeds earlier labels' predictions into later classifiers to use those dependencies.

lessons.title: Ensembles
objectives: Compare bagging, boosting and stacking
Judge when an ensemble is worth its cost
key_points: Bagging averages models trained on bootstrap samples to reduce variance (random forests); boosting trains models in sequence, each correcting the errors of the ones before, to reduce bias (gradient boosting).

Stacking trains a final model on base models' predictions; scikit-learn's StackingClassifier uses cross-validated predictions, so the final model never learns from predictions made on the base models' own training rows.
Ensembles help most when members are accurate and make different errors; averaging near-identical models adds cost without benefit.
Soft voting averages predicted probabilities and needs reasonably calibrated members; hard voting takes the majority class.
The costs are real: more compute for training and serving, higher latency, bigger artefacts and harder explanations, so compare with the best single model before adopting an ensemble.

lessons.title: Cascade
objectives: Design a cascade for a rare subgroup or a cost-saving first stage
Train and evaluate a cascade without leaking labels into routing
key_points: A cascade splits a problem into stages: an early model decides which later model handles each case, for example recognising unusual catering orders and sending them to a model of their own.
Use it when a rare subgroup behaves differently and is drowned out in one model, or when a cheap first stage can settle easy cases and pass only hard ones to an expensive model or a person.
Train each stage on what it will see in production: route training rows to the second-stage models with the first stage's out-of-fold predictions, not with the true labels.
Errors compound across stages and there are more models to train, version and monitor; evaluate the cascade end to end, and compare it with a flexible single model, which can sometimes do as well.
Treat a cascade as one unit: train, test and deploy its stages together in a pipeline, so a change to one stage is always tested with the others.

"""Lab 3: problem representation patterns: reframing, multilabel, ensembles and a cascade."""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from sklearn.datasets import load_breast_cancer
from sklearn.ensemble import (HistGradientBoostingClassifier, HistGradientBoostingRegressor,
                              RandomForestClassifier, StackingClassifier)
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression, LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score, hamming_loss, accuracy_score, mean_absolute_error
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_predict, cross_val_score
from sklearn.multioutput import MultiOutputClassifier
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import MultiLabelBinarizer, StandardScaler
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- A. Reframing
def river_orders(seed, n=4000):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    across = rng.rand(n) < 0.5                      # the address is across the river
    bridge_closed = rng.rand(n) < 0.4               # not known when the order is placed
    distance = np.round(rng.uniform(1, 6, n), 2)
    minutes = 12 + 3 * distance + across * np.where(bridge_closed, 30, 2) + rng.normal(0, 3, n)
    return pd.DataFrame({"across_river": across.astype(int), "distance_km": distance, "minutes": minutes.round(1)})


def part_a():
    train = river_orders(1)
    X = train[["across_river", "distance_km"]]
    reg = LinearRegression().fit(X, train["minutes"])
    edges = [0, 30, 45, 60, np.inf]
    labels = ["<30", "30-45", "45-60", "60+"]
    # TODO: reframe: cut minutes into the four buckets with pd.cut(train["minutes"], edges, labels=labels,
    #       right=False), then fit LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000) on X and the buckets
    print(f"A. Regression says {reg.predict(pd.DataFrame({'across_river': [1], 'distance_km': [3.0]}))[0]:.1f} "
          "minutes; TODO: reframe as buckets")
    return
    order = pd.DataFrame({"across_river": [1], "distance_km": [3.0]})
    proba = dict(zip(clf.classes_, clf.predict_proba(order)[0].round(2)))
    print(f"A. Order across the river, 3 km: regression says {reg.predict(order)[0]:.1f} minutes")
    print(f"   Reframed as buckets: {[(b, float(proba[b])) for b in labels]}")
    print(f"   P(45 minutes or more) = {proba['45-60'] + proba['60+']:.2f}")
    similar = train[(train["across_river"] == 1) & train["distance_km"].between(2.5, 3.5)]
    near = (similar["minutes"] - reg.predict(order)[0]).abs().le(5).mean()
    print(f"   Similar past orders within 5 minutes of the regression's answer: {near:.0%}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- B. Multilabel
TOPICS = {
    "billing": ["I was charged twice", "my invoice shows the wrong amount", "the card payment failed"],
    "login": ["I cannot log in", "the password reset email never arrived", "my account is locked"],
    "delivery": ["the parcel is late", "the courier went to the wrong address", "the box arrived damaged"],
    "refund": ["I want my money back", "please refund the order", "when will the refund arrive"],
}


def tickets(seed, n=1500):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    texts, tags = [], []
    for _ in range(n):
        chosen = sorted(rng.choice(list(TOPICS), rng.choice([1, 2, 3], p=[0.5, 0.35, 0.15]), replace=False))
        text = " and ".join(rng.choice(TOPICS[t]) for t in chosen)
        if rng.rand() < 0.15:                     # some customers mention a topic without it being the issue
            text += " " + rng.choice(["unlike last time when", "my friend said"]) + " " + rng.choice(
                TOPICS[rng.choice(list(TOPICS))])
        texts.append(text)
        tags.append(chosen)
    return texts, tags


def part_b():
    texts, tags = tickets(1)
    test_texts, test_tags = tickets(2, 500)
    # TODO: mlb = MultiLabelBinarizer(); Y = mlb.fit_transform(tags) gives one 0/1 column per label.
    #       Fit make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(), MultiOutputClassifier(LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)))
    #       on texts and Y, then delete the return below
    return
    pred = model.predict(test_texts)
    Y_test = mlb.transform(test_tags)
    print(f"B. Multilabel: labels {[str(c) for c in mlb.classes_]}")
    print(f"   Hamming loss {hamming_loss(Y_test, pred):.3f}  subset accuracy {accuracy_score(Y_test, pred):.3f}"
          f"  micro F1 {f1_score(Y_test, pred, average='micro'):.3f}")
    new = ["my account is locked and the card payment failed", "the box arrived damaged"]
    for text, row in zip(new, model.predict(new)):
        print(f"   {text!r} -> {[str(c) for c in mlb.classes_[row == 1]]}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- C. Ensembles
def part_c():
    X, y = load_breast_cancer(return_X_y=True)
    scaled_lr = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))
    models = {
        "single decision tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
        "bagging (random forest)": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
        "boosting (hist gradient)": HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
        "stacking (3 models -> LR)": StackingClassifier(
            [("lr", scaled_lr), ("rf", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0)),
             ("gb", HistGradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0))],
            final_estimator=LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000), cv=5),
    }
    for name, model in models.items():
        scores = cross_val_score(model, X, y, cv=5, scoring="roc_auc")
        print(f"C. {name:<26} AUC {scores.mean():.3f}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- D. Cascade
def kitchen_orders(seed, n=6000):
    rng = np.random.RandomState(seed)
    bulk = rng.rand(n) < 0.06                       # catering orders: flagged by the kitchen only afterwards
    items = np.where(bulk, rng.randint(8, 50, n), rng.randint(1, 16, n))
    value = np.round(items * np.where(bulk, rng.uniform(9, 16, n), rng.uniform(5, 12, n)) + rng.normal(0, 10, n), 2)
    distance = np.round(rng.gamma(2, 2.5, n), 2)
    minutes = np.where(bulk, 35 + 1.1 * items + 2.0 * distance, 12 + 0.8 * items + 3.0 * distance) \
        + rng.normal(0, 4, n)
    return pd.DataFrame({"items": items, "order_value": value, "distance_km": distance,
                         "bulk": bulk.astype(int), "minutes": minutes.round(1)})


def part_d():
    train, test = kitchen_orders(1), kitchen_orders(2)
    X = ["items", "order_value", "distance_km"]
    bulk_rows = test["bulk"] == 1

    def mae(pred):
        return (f"all {mean_absolute_error(test['minutes'], pred):5.2f}  "
                f"bulk {mean_absolute_error(test['minutes'][bulk_rows], pred[bulk_rows]):5.2f}")

    single = LinearRegression().fit(train[X], train["minutes"]).predict(test[X])
    print(f"D. single linear model            {mae(single)}")

    # stage 1 recognises catering orders; stage 2 has one model per route
    # TODO: stage 1: a LogisticRegression that predicts train["bulk"] from X. Decide which TRAINING rows
    #       it routes to the catering model with out-of-fold probabilities:
    #       cross_val_predict(stage1, train[X], train["bulk"], cv=5, method="predict_proba")[:, 1] >= 0.5
    #       then fit stage1 on all training rows.
    # TODO: stage 2: one LinearRegression on the rows routed as typical, one on the rows routed as catering.
    # TODO: route the test rows with stage1 (probability >= 0.5) and take each row's prediction from its model.
    route = np.zeros(len(test), dtype=bool)
    cascade = single
    print(f"   cascade: classifier + 2 linear  {mae(cascade)}   "
          f"(routes {route.mean():.1%} as catering, {(route == bulk_rows).mean():.1%} correctly)")

    flexible = HistGradientBoostingRegressor(random_state=0).fit(train[X], train["minutes"]).predict(test[X])
    print(f"   single gradient boosting        {mae(flexible)}")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    part_a()
    part_b()
    part_c()
    part_d()

modules.title: Training Optimisation Patterns
modules.summary: Patterns for the training loop: overfit on purpose when the input space is closed, checkpoint so long runs survive failures, transfer what a model has learnt to a new task, and distribute training across workers.

lessons.title: Useful overfitting
objectives: Recognise when fitting the training data exactly is the goal
Use overfitting a tiny batch as a debugging check
key_points: Overfitting is usually a fault, but when a model will only ever see inputs from a known, finite space and the labels are exact, the aim is to fit every example perfectly, with no regularisation and no held-out set.
The typical use replaces a slow deterministic computation with a fast model, such as a physics simulation or a lookup table approximated over a grid that covers every input it will receive.
The limits are strict: between grid points a memorising model only approximates, and outside the covered range it can be badly wrong, so check how the model will be queried before relying on it.
Overfitting a tiny batch is a debugging check: a model that can't reach near-perfect training accuracy on a handful of examples has a bug in its code, data or set-up.
If inputs can be noisy or new, normal practice applies: validation data, regularisation and early stopping.

lessons.title: Checkpoints
objectives: List what a checkpoint must contain to resume training exactly
Write checkpoints safely and use them for early stopping
key_points: A checkpoint saves the full training state at intervals: parameters, optimiser state (such as the step count behind a learning-rate schedule), the epoch, the random-number generator state and the best score so far.
Checkpoints let a long job survive crashes and pre-emptible machines by resuming from the last save; the weights saved for serving aren't enough to resume the same run.
Restore the random-number generator too: a resumed run that reshuffles with a fresh generator sees the data in a different order and ends with different weights.
Write each checkpoint to a temporary file and rename it over the old one (os.replace is atomic), so a crash in the middle of a write never corrupts the last good checkpoint.
Early stopping uses checkpoints: evaluate on validation data after each epoch, keep the best checkpoint, and stop when the score hasn't improved for a set number of epochs, the patience.
In PyTorch, torch.save stores a dictionary of the model's and the optimiser's state_dict(); scikit-learn estimators with partial_fit train incrementally and can be checkpointed with joblib.

lessons.title: Transfer learning
objectives: Compare feature extraction and fine-tuning
Decide whether transfer helps by measuring it
key_points: Transfer learning reuses a model trained on a large dataset for a related task with less data: keep its layers as a frozen feature extractor and train a new output layer, or fine-tune some or all layers at a low learning rate.
It works because early and middle layers learn general features, such as strokes and shapes in images or word meanings in text, that are useful beyond the original task.
Feature extraction is cheaper and safer with very little labelled data; fine-tuning adapts more but needs more data and care so the new data doesn't overwrite what the base model learnt.
Transfer helps only when the source and target are related, so measure it against a model trained from scratch on the same labelled data; when it makes things worse, that's negative transfer.
Record the base model, its version and its licence in the new model's lineage: pretrained models from hubs such as Hugging Face come with licences, and some restrict how they may be used.

lessons.title: Distribution strategy
objectives: Compare data, model and pipeline parallelism
Explain how gradients are combined in synchronous data parallelism
key_points: A distribution strategy spreads training over several devices or machines when one is too slow or the model is too big for a single device's memory.

Data parallelism copies the model to every worker, gives each a slice of every batch and averages the gradients; with synchronous all-reduce, each step waits for all workers and matches training on the whole batch on one machine.
Weight each worker's gradient by the number of examples it processed: a plain average over unequal shards gives the small shards too much say.
Model parallelism splits the model itself across devices when it doesn't fit on one; pipeline parallelism puts groups of layers on different devices and keeps them busy with micro-batches.

PyTorch's DistributedDataParallel and TensorFlow's tf.distribute.MirroredStrategy implement synchronous data parallelism; more workers mean a bigger global batch, often with an adjusted learning rate and a warm-up.
Communication costs make the speed-up less than linear in the number of workers, so measure before adding hardware; on one machine, n_jobs runs cross-validation folds and forest trees in parallel.

"""Lab 4: training patterns: useful overfitting, checkpoints, transfer learning and data parallelism."""

import os
from pathlib import Path

import joblib
import numpy as np
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression, SGDClassifier
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeRegressor


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- A. Useful overfitting
def stopping_distance(speed_kmh, friction, reaction_s=1.0):
    v = speed_kmh / 3.6
    return v * reaction_s + v ** 2 / (2 * friction * 9.81)


def part_a():
    speeds, frictions = np.arange(20, 131, 5), np.round(np.arange(0.2, 0.91, 0.05), 2)
    grid = np.array([(s, f) for s in speeds for f in frictions])            # every input the model will get
    y = stopping_distance(grid[:, 0], grid[:, 1])
    tree = DecisionTreeRegressor(random_state=0).fit(grid, y)              # no depth limit, no validation set
    print(f"A. Physics table: {len(grid)} inputs; training error {np.abs(tree.predict(grid) - y).max():.3f} m")
    between = np.array([(s + 2.5, f + 0.025) for s in speeds[:-1] for f in frictions[:-1]])
    err_between = np.abs(tree.predict(between) - stopping_distance(between[:, 0], between[:, 1])).mean()
    outside = np.array([(s, 0.5) for s in range(140, 161, 5)])
    err_outside = np.abs(tree.predict(outside) - stopping_distance(outside[:, 0], outside[:, 1])).mean()
    print(f"   Mean error between grid points {err_between:.1f} m; beyond 130 km/h {err_outside:.1f} m")
    X, digits_y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
    tiny = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=2000, random_state=0).fit(X[:16] / 16, digits_y[:16])
    print(f"   Debugging check, overfit 16 examples: training accuracy {tiny.score(X[:16] / 16, digits_y[:16]):.2f}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- B. Checkpoints
CHECKPOINT = Path("checkpoints/sgd.joblib")


def save_checkpoint(state):
    CHECKPOINT.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    # TODO: write the state to a temporary file next to CHECKPOINT (CHECKPOINT.with_suffix(".tmp")) with
    #       joblib.dump, then move it over CHECKPOINT with os.replace, which is atomic
    joblib.dump(state, CHECKPOINT)


def train(X, y, X_val, y_val, epochs=8, crash_after=None, resume=False, fresh_rng=False):
    CHECKPOINT.parent.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    if resume:
        state = joblib.load(CHECKPOINT)
        model, start, rng = state["model"], state["epoch"] + 1, np.random.default_rng(0)
        if not fresh_rng:
            pass   # TODO: restore the shuffling sequence: rng.bit_generator.state = state["rng_state"]
        best = state["best"]
    else:
        model, start, rng = SGDClassifier(loss="log_loss", random_state=0), 1, np.random.default_rng(0)
        best = {"score": -1.0, "epoch": 0}
    for epoch in range(start, epochs + 1):
        order = rng.permutation(len(y))
        model.partial_fit(X[order], y[order], classes=np.arange(10))
        score = model.score(X_val, y_val)
        if score > best["score"]:
            best = {"score": score, "epoch": epoch}
            joblib.dump(model, "checkpoints/best.joblib")      # keep the best model for early stopping
        save_checkpoint({"model": model, "epoch": epoch, "rng_state": rng.bit_generator.state, "best": best})
        if epoch == crash_after:
            raise RuntimeError(f"machine pre-empted after epoch {epoch}")
    return model, best


def part_b():
    X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
    X = X / 16
    X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val = X[:1400], y[:1400], X[1400:], y[1400:]
    reference, best = train(X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val)
    print(f"B. Uninterrupted: 8 epochs, best validation accuracy {best['score']:.3f} at epoch {best['epoch']}")
    try:
        train(X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val, crash_after=3)
    except RuntimeError as e:
        print(f"   Crash: {e}; last checkpoint is epoch {joblib.load(CHECKPOINT)['epoch']}")
    resumed, _ = train(X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val, resume=True)
    print(f"   Resumed from the checkpoint: same weights as uninterrupted: {np.array_equal(resumed.coef_, reference.coef_)}")
    try:
        train(X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val, crash_after=3)                  # crash again at the same point
    except RuntimeError:
        pass
    wrong, _ = train(X_tr, y_tr, X_val, y_val, resume=True, fresh_rng=True)
    print(f"   Resumed without the RNG state: same weights: {np.array_equal(wrong.coef_, reference.coef_)}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- C. Transfer learning
def part_c():
    X, y = load_digits(return_X_y=True)
    X = X / 16
    source, target = np.arange(1000), np.arange(1000, len(y))      # different images for the two tasks
    base = MLPClassifier(hidden_layer_sizes=(64,), max_iter=1000, random_state=0).fit(X[source], y[source])

    def features(data):                                  # the base network's hidden layer, frozen
        # TODO: the hidden layer's activations: ReLU of data @ base.coefs_[0] + base.intercepts_[0]
        return data

    Xt, even = X[target], (y[target] % 2 == 0).astype(int)  # the new task: is the digit even?
    few = np.random.RandomState(0).choice(len(target), 40, replace=False)
    rest = np.setdiff1d(np.arange(len(target)), few)
    raw = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(Xt[few], even[few]).score(Xt[rest], even[rest])
    transfer = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000).fit(features(Xt[few]), even[few]).score(features(Xt[rest]), even[rest])
    print(f"C. 'Is it even?' from 40 labelled images: raw pixels {raw:.3f}, "
          f"frozen features of a digit classifier {transfer:.3f}")


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- D. Distribution strategy
def gradient(w, X, y):
    p = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ w)))
    return X.T @ (p - y) / len(y)                       # mean gradient of the log loss


def part_d():
    rng = np.random.RandomState(0)
    X, w = rng.normal(size=(1000, 5)), rng.normal(size=5)
    y = (rng.rand(1000) < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(X @ np.array([1.0, -2.0, 0.5, 0.0, 1.5]))))).astype(float)
    full = gradient(w, X, y)
    equal = np.array_split(np.arange(1000), 4)
    averaged = np.mean([gradient(w, X[i], y[i]) for i in equal], axis=0)
    print(f"D. 4 workers, equal shards: averaged gradient equals the full-batch gradient: {np.allclose(averaged, full)}")
    sizes = np.split(np.arange(1000), [100, 400, 600])           # shards of 100, 300, 200 and 400 rows
    naive = np.mean([gradient(w, X[i], y[i]) for i in sizes], axis=0)
    weighted = naive    # TODO: weight each shard's gradient by its number of rows, then divide by 1000

modules.summary: Serve models with stateless functions and batch jobs, make the process repeatable with workflow pipelines, and build training data with point-in-time joins, the core of the feature store pattern.

lessons.title: Stateless serving function
objectives: Design a stateless prediction service with a validated interface
Use keyed predictions so batch callers can match results to inputs
key_points: Export the trained model with its preprocessing as one artefact, and wrap it in a function that takes a request and returns a prediction, keeping nothing between calls.
Statelessness lets a platform run many identical copies behind a load balancer, add or remove copies with demand, and restart any copy without losing anything.
Keep changing state outside the function: per-customer features come from a database or feature store, and the model is loaded once at start-up and only read afterwards.
Treat the interface as a contract: validate inputs with a schema (FastAPI uses Pydantic models and rejects bad input with a 422 response) and return the model version with every prediction.
Keyed predictions: accept a client-supplied key with each instance and echo it back, so a caller sending a batch can match results to inputs whatever order they are processed in.

lessons.title: Batch serving
objectives: Choose batch serving for the right workloads
Share the prediction code between batch and online serving
key_points: Batch serving runs the model over many inputs as a scheduled job and stores the results, for predictions needed for many items but not instantly, such as nightly churn scores for every customer.
Use the same exported model and the same prediction function as the online service, in a job built for throughput rather than latency.
Serve stored results with a fast lookup by key, and fall back to a default or to the online service for keys the last run didn't score, such as customers who joined since.
Batch results are only as fresh as the last run: schedule runs by how fast inputs change, and store the model version and the as-of time with every prediction.
The Lambda architecture combines a batch layer, recomputed periodically over all the data, with a speed layer that updates results from recent events.

lessons.title: Workflow pipeline
objectives: Split an ML process into steps with declared inputs and outputs
Explain content-addressed caching and the danger of undeclared inputs
key_points: The workflow pipeline pattern splits the ML process into steps with defined inputs and outputs, such as building the training set, training, testing the service and batch scoring, and runs them in order on every change.
Each step can be rerun, cached, tested and scaled on its own, and the pipeline records which inputs produced which outputs: the lineage.
Content-addressed caching skips a step when the hash of its inputs and code is unchanged; an undeclared input, such as a module the step imports, lets a stale result be served from the cache.
Orchestrators such as Kubeflow Pipelines, TFX, Apache Airflow and Dagster run steps as containers or tasks and track their runs; a short script that hashes inputs applies the same idea locally.
Make steps idempotent, so running a step twice with the same inputs gives the same outputs; that makes retries and caching safe.

lessons.title: Feature store
objectives: Explain the problems a feature store solves
Build a point-in-time correct training set with an ASOF join
key_points: A feature store manages features as shared, versioned assets: each is defined once, computed once, and served to training from an offline store of history and to prediction from a low-latency online store of latest values.
It tackles training-serving skew (one definition used in both places), duplicated feature work across teams, and point-in-time correctness.

A point-in-time join gives each training example the feature values as they were at its timestamp. Joining the latest values instead leaks the future, such as orders dropping to zero after a customer churned.
DuckDB's ASOF JOIN, like similar joins in warehouses and feature-store libraries, finds for each label the latest feature row at or before the label's time.
Feast is an open-source feature store and cloud ML platforms offer managed ones; a small team with one model may need only shared feature code and a point-in-time SQL join.

"""Write customer_features.csv (weekly feature snapshots) and labels.csv (one churn label per customer).
Fixed seed, so everyone gets the same rows.  Run: python make_churn_data.py"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.RandomState(8)
weeks = pd.date_range("2025-01-06", periods=20, freq="7D")           # Monday snapshots
rows, labels = [], []
for c in range(1, 601):
    plan = rng.choice(["free", "plus", "pro"], p=[0.5, 0.35, 0.15])
    tenure = int(rng.randint(1, 48))
    engagement = rng.gamma(2, 2) * {"free": 0.7, "plus": 1.0, "pro": 1.4}[plan]
    label_week = int(rng.randint(6, 18))
    risk = -1.0 - 0.35 * engagement - 0.03 * tenure + {"free": 0.6, "plus": 0.0, "pro": -0.4}[plan]
    churned = rng.rand() < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-(risk + 1.2)))
    for w, t in enumerate(weeks):
        active = not (churned and w > label_week + 1)                 # churners stop ordering soon after
        orders = int(rng.poisson(engagement * (1.0 if active else 0.0)))
        tickets = int(rng.poisson(0.3 + (0.8 if churned and abs(w - label_week) <= 2 else 0.0)))
        rows.append((f"C{c:04d}", t.date(), orders, tickets, tenure + w // 4, plan))
    label_time = weeks[label_week] + pd.Timedelta(days=int(rng.randint(1, 7)), hours=10)
    labels.append((f"C{c:04d}", label_time, int(churned)))

pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["customer_id", "feature_time", "orders_30d", "tickets_30d", "tenure_months", "plan"]
             ).to_csv("customer_features.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame(labels, columns=["customer_id", "label_time", "churned_next_30d"]).sort_values(
    "label_time", kind="stable").to_csv("labels.csv", index=False)
print(f"customer_features.csv: {len(rows)} snapshots; labels.csv: {len(labels)} labels, "
      f"{np.mean([l[2] for l in labels]):.1%} churned")

"""Build training sets two ways, a naive latest-value join and a point-in-time (ASOF) join, and compare them."""

import duckdb
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, StandardScaler

FEATURES = ["orders_30d", "tickets_30d", "tenure_months", "plan"]
SPLIT = "2025-03-24"            # labels before this date train the model; later ones test it

NAIVE = """
    SELECT l.*, f.feature_time, f.orders_30d, f.tickets_30d, f.tenure_months, f.plan
    FROM labels l
    JOIN (SELECT * FROM features QUALIFY row_number() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY feature_time DESC) = 1) f
      USING (customer_id)"""

# TODO: the point-in-time join: for each label, the latest snapshot at or before its label_time.
#       DuckDB's ASOF JOIN does exactly this:  ... FROM labels l ASOF JOIN features f
#       ON l.customer_id = f.customer_id AND l.label_time >= f.feature_time
POINT_IN_TIME = NAIVE


def connect():
    con = duckdb.connect()
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE features AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('customer_features.csv', header=true)")
    con.execute("CREATE TABLE labels AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('labels.csv', header=true)")
    return con


def build(con, query):
    return con.sql(query).df().sort_values("customer_id", kind="stable").reset_index(drop=True)


def model():
    prep = ColumnTransformer([("num", StandardScaler(), FEATURES[:3]),
                              ("cat", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"), ["plan"])])
    return make_pipeline(prep, LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))


def split(df):
    return df[df["label_time"] < SPLIT], df[df["label_time"] >= SPLIT]


def main():
    con = connect()
    naive, pit = build(con, NAIVE), build(con, POINT_IN_TIME)
    future = (naive["feature_time"] > naive["label_time"].dt.date).sum()
    print(f"Naive join: {future} of {len(naive)} labels got features from after the label time")
    print(f"Point-in-time join: {(pit['feature_time'] > pit['label_time'].dt.date).sum()} of {len(pit)}")

    naive_train, naive_test = split(naive)
    pit_train, pit_test = split(pit)
    m_naive = model().fit(naive_train[FEATURES], naive_train["churned_next_30d"])
    m_pit = model().fit(pit_train[FEATURES], pit_train["churned_next_30d"])

    def auc(m, df):
        return roc_auc_score(df["churned_next_30d"], m.predict_proba(df[FEATURES])[:, 1])

    print(f"Naive model, offline test AUC:            {auc(m_naive, naive_test):.3f}")
    print(f"Naive model, on features as of label time: {auc(m_naive, pit_test):.3f}   <- what production would see")
    print(f"Point-in-time model, test AUC:             {auc(m_pit, pit_test):.3f}")
    pit.to_parquet("training_set.parquet", index=False)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Train the churn model on the point-in-time training set and save it as one versioned bundle."""

from pathlib import Path

import joblib
import pandas as pd

from point_in_time import FEATURES, model

VERSION = "churn-v1"


def main():
    data = pd.read_parquet("training_set.parquet")
    pipeline = model().fit(data[FEATURES], data["churned_next_30d"])
    Path("models").mkdir(exist_ok=True)

    print(f"Saved models/{VERSION}.joblib: preprocessing and model in one artefact, trained on {len(data)} rows")

    main()

"""A stateless serving function: load the bundle once, validate requests, return keyed predictions."""

from contextlib import asynccontextmanager
from typing import Literal

import joblib
import pandas as pd
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field

MODEL_PATH = "models/churn-v1.joblib"
bundle = {}                                   # filled once at start-up, then only read


class Instance(BaseModel):
    # TODO: validate every field: plan must be "free", "plus" or "pro" (Literal[...]), and the three counts
    #       must be whole numbers of at least 0 (int = Field(ge=0))
    key: str = Field(min_length=1, max_length=64)          # the caller's own ID, echoed back
    plan: str
    orders_30d: float
    tickets_30d: float
    tenure_months: float


class PredictRequest(BaseModel):
    instances: list[Instance] = Field(min_length=1, max_length=1000)


def predict_rows(model_bundle, rows):
    """Shared by the API and the batch job, so both apply exactly the same pipeline."""
    return model_bundle["pipeline"].predict_proba(rows[model_bundle["features"]])[:, 1]


@asynccontextmanager
async def lifespan(app):
    bundle.update(joblib.load(MODEL_PATH))
    yield


app = FastAPI(title="churn model", lifespan=lifespan)


@app.get("/health")
def health():
    return {"status": "ok", "model_version": bundle["version"]}


@app.post("/predict")
def predict(request: PredictRequest):
    rows = pd.DataFrame([i.model_dump() for i in request.instances])
    probabilities = predict_rows(bundle, rows)
    # TODO: return the model version and, for each instance, its key with its churn probability rounded to 4
    #       places: {"model_version": ..., "predictions": [{"key": ..., "churn_probability": ...}, ...]}
    return {"predictions": [round(float(p), 4) for p in probabilities]}

from fastapi.testclient import TestClient

from serve import app

ROWS = [
    {"key": "order-b", "plan": "free", "orders_30d": 0, "tickets_30d": 3, "tenure_months": 2},

]


def test_health_reports_the_model_version():

def test_predictions_keep_the_callers_keys_and_order():

"""Batch serving: score every customer's latest features with the same function the API uses."""

import duckdb
import joblib

from serve import MODEL_PATH, predict_rows

AS_OF = "2025-05-19"


def main():
    model_bundle = joblib.load(MODEL_PATH)
    con = duckdb.connect()

                     FROM 'churn_scores.parquet' GROUP BY model_version""").fetchall())


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""A workflow pipeline in miniature: each step declares its inputs and outputs, and is skipped when neither its
inputs nor its code have changed since the last successful run."""

import hashlib
import json
import subprocess
import sys
from pathlib import Path

STEPS = [  # name, script, inputs, outputs
    ("build_training_set", "point_in_time.py", ["customer_features.csv", "labels.csv", "point_in_time.py"],
     ["training_set.parquet"]),
    ("train", "train_bundle.py", ["training_set.parquet", "train_bundle.py"], ["models/churn-v1.joblib"]),
    ("test_service", "-m pytest -q test_serve.py", ["models/churn-v1.joblib", "serve.py", "test_serve.py"], []),
    ("batch_score", "batch_score.py", ["models/churn-v1.joblib", "batch_score.py", "customer_features.csv"],
     ["churn_scores.parquet"]),
]
STATE = Path(".pipeline_state.json")


def fingerprint(paths):
    h = hashlib.sha256()
    for p in paths:
        h.update(p.encode())
        h.update(Path(p).read_bytes())
    return h.hexdigest()


def main():
    state = json.loads(STATE.read_text()) if STATE.exists() else {}
    for name, script, inputs, outputs in STEPS:
        key = fingerprint(inputs)
        if state.get(name) == key and all(Path(o).exists() for o in outputs):
            print(f"{name:<20} cached")
            continue
        result = subprocess.run([sys.executable, *script.split()], capture_output=True, text=True)
        if result.returncode != 0:
            print(f"{name:<20} FAILED\n{result.stdout}{result.stderr}")
            sys.exit(1)
        state[name] = key
        STATE.write_text(json.dumps(state, indent=2))
        print(f"{name:<20} ran")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

"""Write the capstone data: customers.csv, customer_features.csv (weekly snapshots), labels.csv, and
new_referrers.csv (customers who signed up after training, some from referrer sites never seen before).
Fixed seed, so everyone gets the same rows.  Run: python make_capstone_data.py"""

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng = np.random.RandomState(21)
weeks = pd.date_range("2025-01-06", periods=20, freq="7D")
site_quality = rng.normal(0, 0.8, 2500)                  # some referrer sites bring loyal customers, some don't
customers, rows, labels = [], [], []
for c in range(1, 1501):
    plan = rng.choice(["free", "plus", "pro"], p=[0.5, 0.35, 0.15])
    site = int(min(rng.zipf(1.3), 2000)) - 1             # a few big referrers and a long tail
    tenure = int(rng.randint(1, 48))
    engagement = rng.gamma(2, 2) * {"free": 0.7, "plus": 1.0, "pro": 1.4}[plan]
    label_week = int(rng.randint(6, 18))
    risk = -0.2 - 0.35 * engagement - 0.03 * tenure + {"free": 0.6, "plus": 0.0, "pro": -0.4}[plan] \
        - site_quality[site]
    churned = rng.rand() < 1 / (1 + np.exp(-risk))
    customers.append((f"C{c:04d}", f"site-{site:04d}.example", plan))
    for w, t in enumerate(weeks):
        active = not (churned and w > label_week + 1)
        rows.append((f"C{c:04d}", t.date(), int(rng.poisson(engagement * active)),
                     int(rng.poisson(0.3 + (0.8 if churned and abs(w - label_week) <= 2 else 0.0))),
                     tenure + w // 4, plan))
    labels.append((f"C{c:04d}", weeks[label_week] + pd.Timedelta(days=int(rng.randint(1, 7)), hours=10), int(churned)))

new = [(f"N{i:04d}", f"site-{int(rng.choice([rng.randint(0, 50), rng.randint(2000, 2500)])):04d}.example",
        rng.choice(["free", "plus", "pro"]), int(rng.poisson(3)), int(rng.poisson(0.4)), int(rng.randint(1, 4)))
       for i in range(1, 201)]

pd.DataFrame(customers, columns=["customer_id", "referrer", "plan"]).to_csv("customers.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["customer_id", "feature_time", "orders_30d", "tickets_30d", "tenure_months", "plan"]
             ).to_csv("customer_features.csv", index=False)
pd.DataFrame(labels, columns=["customer_id", "label_time", "churned_next_30d"]).sort_values(
    "label_time", kind="stable").to_csv("labels.csv", index=False)
